The Time of Troubles. Between fifteen ninety-eight and sixteen thirteen, Russia endured a period of civil strife, foreign invasion, and dynastic confusion following the death of Tsar Ivan the Terrible. The chaos included succession crises, impostor claimants, Polish-Lithuanian occupation of Moscow, famine, and peasant rebellions, ending only with the election of Mikhail Romanov as tsar and the founding of the Romanov dynasty that would rule Russia until nineteen seventeen.

After Ivan IV's death in fifteen eighty-four, his weak son Feodor I inherited an exhausted realm. Boris Godunov, a powerful regent, consolidated control and was elected tsar after Feodor's death in fifteen ninety-eight, but faced immediate opposition and legitimacy questions. A succession of false claimants emerged, especially the False Dmitri between sixteen oh-three and sixteen oh-five, who claimed to be Ivan's younger son. With Polish-Lithuanian backing, the false Dmitri briefly occupied the throne, highlighting the weakness of Godunov's regime.

Swedish and Polish forces invaded Russia, exploiting the chaos. The Poles occupied Moscow and installed their own puppet tsar. Russia faced fragmentation, famine particularly harsh between sixteen oh-one and sixteen oh-three, and widespread social breakdown. Peasant rebellions erupted, including Cossack uprisings under Stenka Razin. The traditional social hierarchy fractured as nobles, merchants, and peasants vied for advantage during the power vacuum.

The Russian Orthodox Church became a symbol of national continuity. Patriarch Filaret, who later became Mikhail Romanov's father, mobilized religious authority and popular sentiment against foreign occupation and illegitimate rulers. In sixteen thirteen, the Zemsky Sobor, an assembly of estates, elected Mikhail Romanov, a young noble whose mother was the daughter of Tsar Ivan IV's advisor, as tsar. His election restored a sense of legitimate succession and native rule.
